content: The most severe adverse effects associated with nevirapine include hepatitis or hepatic failure, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and hypersensitivity reactions. Hepatitis or hepatic failure may present with symptoms of hypersensitivity, such as severe rash or rash accompanied by fever, general malaise, fatigue, muscle or joint pain, blisters, oral lesions, conjunctivitis, facial swelling, eosinophilia, granulocytopenia, lymphadenopathy, or renal dysfunction. The first 18 weeks of nevirapine therapy are critical, requiring close clinical and laboratory monitoring to identify potentially life-threatening liver or skin reactions. Although the optimal frequency of monitoring during this period is not established, some experts recommend more frequent assessments than once per month. This includes liver enzyme testing before starting the 14-day lead-in period with immediate-release VIRAMUNE, before initiating VIRAMUNE XR, and two weeks after starting VIRAMUNE XR therapy. After the initial 18 weeks, regular clinical and laboratory monitoring should continue throughout treatment. The 14-day lead-in period with immediate-release VIRAMUNE has been shown to reduce the incidence of rash. Patients transitioning from immediate-release VIRAMUNE to VIRAMUNE XR should maintain their ongoing monitoring schedule. Severe and potentially fatal hepatotoxicity, including fulminant and cholestatic hepatitis, hepatic necrosis, and hepatic failure, has been reported in patients treated with nevirapine. The risk of symptomatic liver events is highest during the first six weeks of therapy but remains elevated through the first 18 weeks. Hepatic events can occur at any time during treatment. Some patients may initially present with nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, malaise, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, liver tenderness, or hepatomegaly, with or without abnormal liver enzyme levels. Rash occurs in approximately half of patients with symptomatic liver events, and fever or flu-like symptoms may accompany these events. In some cases, these symptoms progress to hepatic failure, with elevated transaminases, hyperbilirubinemia, hepatic encephalopathy, prolonged partial thromboplastin time, or eosinophilia. Rhabdomyolysis has also been observed in some patients with liver or skin reactions related to nevirapine use. Patients showing signs or symptoms of hepatitis should immediately discontinue nevirapine and undergo medical evaluation, including liver enzyme testing. Transaminase levels should be checked immediately in patients with symptoms suggestive of hepatitis or hypersensitivity reactions, as well as in those who develop a rash during the first 18 weeks of treatment. Physicians and patients should remain vigilant for symptoms of hepatitis, such as fatigue, malaise, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, liver tenderness, or hepatomegaly. Hepatotoxicity should be considered even if transaminase levels are initially normal or alternative diagnoses are possible. If clinical hepatitis or transaminase elevations occur alongside rash or systemic symptoms, nevirapine should be permanently discontinued and not restarted. In some cases, liver injury may progress despite stopping the drug. Women with high CD4+ cell counts are at the greatest risk for hepatic events, including fatal outcomes. Retrospective analyses of clinical trials with immediate-release VIRAMUNE showed that during the first six weeks of treatment, women had a threefold higher risk than men for symptomatic hepatic events, often associated with rash (6% versus 2%). Women with CD4+ counts above 250 cells/mm³ had a 12-fold higher risk of symptomatic liver events compared to those with CD4+ counts below 250 cells/mm³ (11% versus 1%). Men with CD4+ counts above 400 cells/mm³ also had an increased risk (6% versus 1% for men with CD4+ counts below 400 cells/mm³). However, all patients, regardless of gender, CD4+ count, or antiretroviral treatment history, should be monitored for hepatotoxicity, as liver events have been reported across all CD4+ levels. Co-infection with hepatitis B or C and/or elevated transaminase levels at the start of nevirapine therapy increases the risk of symptomatic liver events and asymptomatic transaminase elevations. VIRAMUNE XR is contraindicated for occupational or non-occupational PEP. Patients with hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis may have increased nevirapine trough concentrations and should be closely monitored for drug-induced toxicity. Nevirapine should not be used in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class B or C). VIRAMUNE XR has not been studied in patients with hepatic impairment. Severe and life-threatening skin reactions, including fatal cases, have been reported with nevirapine use, particularly during the first six weeks of therapy. These reactions include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and hypersensitivity reactions characterized by rash, systemic symptoms, and organ dysfunction, including liver failure. Rhabdomyolysis has been observed in some patients with skin or liver reactions. Patients who develop severe skin reactions or hypersensitivity symptoms, such as severe rash, rash with fever, malaise, fatigue, muscle or joint pain, blisters, oral lesions, conjunctivitis, facial swelling, hepatitis, eosinophilia, granulocytopenia, lymphadenopathy, or renal dysfunction, must permanently discontinue nevirapine and seek immediate medical evaluation. Nevirapine should not be restarted in patients who experience severe rash, rash with transaminase elevations, or hypersensitivity reactions. Nevirapine should be permanently discontinued in patients with rash-associated transaminase elevations. Therapy should begin with immediate-release VIRAMUNE at a daily dose for the first 14 days, as this lead-in period reduces the risk of rash. If a patient develops a severe rash or a rash with systemic symptoms, nevirapine should be discontinued. Patients with mild to moderate rash during the lead-in period should not start VIRAMUNE XR until the rash resolves. The lead-in period should not exceed 28 days; if the rash persists, an alternative treatment should be considered. Patients should be closely monitored for any rash, as delayed discontinuation of nevirapine may lead to more severe reactions. Women are at higher risk than men for developing rash with nevirapine. In a clinical trial, the use of prednisone (40 mg daily for the first 14 days of nevirapine therapy) was associated with an increased incidence and severity of rash. Therefore, prednisone is not recommended for preventing nevirapine-associated rash. VIRAMUNE XR should not be used as monotherapy for HIV-1 treatment or added as a single agent to a failing regimen, as resistant virus rapidly emerges. When selecting new antiretroviral agents to combine with nevirapine, the potential for cross-resistance should be considered. When discontinuing a regimen containing VIRAMUNE XR, the long half-life of nevirapine must be taken into account. If antiretrovirals with shorter half-lives are stopped simultaneously, low plasma concentrations of nevirapine may persist for a week or longer, increasing the risk of viral resistance. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy, including nevirapine. During the initial phase of treatment, patients with immune recovery may develop inflammatory responses to latent or residual opportunistic infections, such as Mycobacterium avium, cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, or tuberculosis, which may require further evaluation and treatment. Autoimmune disorders, such as Graves’ disease, polymyositis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, have also been reported in the context of immune reconstitution. These conditions may have a delayed onset, occurring months after starting therapy. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. This may manifest as central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, or a Cushingoid appearance. The mechanism and long-term consequences of these changes are not fully understood, and a causal relationship has not been established.
